newsitem.title: INDIA: Police teargas anti-poll protestors in Kashmir.
newsitem.headline: Police teargas anti-poll protestors in Kashmir.

text.p: Police teargassed protestors during a strike called by separatists on Sunday as Kashmir prepared for another set of assembly polls.

Supporters of some candidates hid their identities with masks as they canvassed for votes in the election, which is the first in nine years and is opposed by separatist rebels fighting against the Moslem majority region's inclusion in Hindu-dominated India. Indian security forces were concentrated in the 34 assembly constituencies that go to the polls on Monday, which will be the second day of a four-stage vote.
Separatist groups held sporadic demonstrations in Srinagar, summer capital of the state of Jammu and Kashmir, said Javed Ahmed Mir, a leader of Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front.
"We shouted anti-Indian slogans and protested against the elections," Mir told Reuters.
Police said they lobbed teargas cannisters on the demonstrators in Srinagar's Maisooma district. Mir said police also opened fire in the air but no one was injured.
Mir was released from jail two days ago after three days in detention. He said police have detained other senior leaders of the separatist Hurriyat Conference for the last three days.
Separatist leaders said Hurriyat chairman Moulvi Mohammad Farooq was kept under house arrest by police.

The 30-party Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference was awaiting a response to its call for a two-day strike by businesses while Moslem militants continued to enforce a closure of government offices, schools and banks which started on August 24.

Anti-Indian groups, which seek a separate nation or a merger with neighbouring Pakistan, have accused the government of intimidating people to vote. India says its forces only offers protection to voters from militant threats.

"An election in which political supporters wear masks and people are coerced to cast their vote with all kinds of threats is a laughable way to solve Kashmir's problems," Hurriyat spokesman Abdul Ghani told Reuters.
Election to the 87-seat assembly has been marred by clashes in which more than 20 political workers have died.
India claimed success after the 26 constituencies voted on September 7.
Politicians said security forces had not deterred rival groups and separatists from attacking opponents.
"The fact that political supporters are forced to wear masks does suggest an element of fear," a defence spokesman told Reuters. "But their percentage is low. It isn't so alarming."

India, which controls two-thirds of the region, does not recognise Pakistan-held Azad, or "Free", Kashmir and keeps 23 seats vacant in the Jammu and Kashmir state assembly. Pakistan denies Indian charges that it arms Kashmiri guerrillas.
India called the polls after major political parties agreed it was the only way to revive democracy in the state.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in the violence in 1990, when the then state chief minister Farooq Abdullah was forced out and direct rule by New Delhi imposed.

Abdullah's National Conference party boycotted parliamentary elections in May but agreed to contest the local elections after New Delhi agreed to open talks on extensive autonomy for Kashmir with the new state government.
Abdullah, who survived an assassination attempt last week, had objected to the presence of government-backed armed militia groups in Kashmir, saying they were a hindrance to the polls.
But sources in the security forces say his party has won over some of the militia leaders as had the Congress party of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party is also in the fray in the elections. Voting in the remaining constituencies is scheduled for September 21 and 30.
